newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Easing of ivory trade ban could help elephants-WWF.
newsitem.headline: Easing of ivory trade ban could help elephants-WWF.

text.p: The World Wide Fund for Nature said on Friday a global forum's easing of an ivory trade ban could be a "blessing in disguise" that will help preserve elephants.

In Harare, the forum on endangered species on Thursday authorised a relaxation of the seven-year-old ban to allow Zimbabwe, Namibia and Botswana conditionally to sell ivory to Japan from their "excess" elephant herds.

Some conservationists warned this could lead to "an elephant holocaust" and open the floodgates to smuggling of stockpiles from Hong Kong, once the centre of the world ivory market where carved-ivory is still widely sold.
But the World Wide Fund for Nature, billed as the world's largest conservationist pressure group, disputed such doomsday scenarios for the elephant.
"This may be a blessing in disguise for the elephants for the money from this renewed trade will be used for their conservation," said the Fund's Hong Kong representative, Alex Yau Shuk-Kau.

"I don't think it will open the floodgates. It must be strictly controlled. It will be subject to international scrutiny. It must only concern stockpiles. No (extra) elephants will be killed to provide ivory," she said.

The U.S. and some European Union members led a strong world lobby -- which included several African states -- against easing the 1989 blanket ban in ivory trade, arguing that it would rekindle poaching and put elephants at risk.

But Zimbabwe, Botswana and Namibia argued for ivory trade, saying that their combined elephant herd of about 150,000 has been growing steadily and was doing so even before the ban. Jill Robinson, director of the International Fund for Animal Welfare China, said: "It's a tragic day for elephants. It just makes one incredibly nervous to have trade opened anywhere in the world."
Yau conceded that Japan's trade controls were lax but disputed Robinson's pessimistic prognosis.
"If poaching or smuggling is reported to be on the increase, the ban will be put in place again. I don't think there will be an elephant holocaust anywhere," she told Reuters.
She was convinced the partial lifting would not affect the status of the 286 tonnes of ivory legally stockpiled in Hong Kong.
These can only be sold within the British colony that is being handed back to China on June 30 and she said: "In Hong Kong, we have some of the most stringent legislation in the world."
